full_text_en:
Yancheng Aokang Food Co., Ltd., Dongtai Branch v. Yancheng Dongtai Administration for Industry and Commerce — dispute over administrative penalty for food safety

【Ruling Summary】

A food label is the text, graphics, symbols, and all descriptive matter on food packaging. If the food label or food instructions specifically emphasize the addition or presence of one or more valuable or characteristic ingredients or components, the amount or content of the emphasized ingredient or component shall be indicated.

Pursuant to Article 86 of the Food Safety Law, where an enterprise operates food that specifically emphasizes a certain ingredient or component without indicating the amount or content added, such operation constitutes the operation of food with labels or instructions that do not comply with the provisions of the Food Safety Law. In such cases, in addition to confiscating the illegal income, the illegally operated food, and the tools, equipment, raw materials, and other articles used for the illegal operation, a fine of not less than two times but not more than five times the value of the goods shall be imposed if the value of the goods exceeds RMB 10,000.

Plaintiff: Yancheng Aokang Food Co., Ltd., Dongtai Branch, domiciled at Heduo Road, Taicheng Town, Dongtai City, Jiangsu Province.
Legal Representative: Wang Lei, General Manager of the Branch.

Defendant: Yancheng Dongtai Administration for Industry and Commerce, domiciled at Fanggong North Road, Taicheng Town, Dongtai City, Jiangsu Province.
Legal Representative: Zhang Liuqi, Director of the Administration.

The plaintiff, Yancheng Aokang Food Co., Ltd., Dongtai Branch (hereinafter referred to as Aokang Company), dissatisfied with the Administrative Penalty Decision No. [2012] 298 (hereinafter referred to as the Penalty Decision) issued by the defendant, Yancheng Dongtai Administration for Industry and Commerce (hereinafter referred to as Dongtai AIC), initiated legal proceedings before the Dongtai People's Court.

The plaintiff, Aokang Company, alleged: 1. The factual determination in the Penalty Decision was erroneous. The term "Olive Fragrance" on the label of the "Golden Arowana" brand Olive Fragrance Edible Blend Oil operated by the plaintiff was an objective description of the product's physical attributes, not an emphasis on the ingredient of olive oil. Olive oil is an ordinary edible oil ingredient and not a valuable or characteristic ingredient, so there was no need to indicate its content or amount added. The defendant Dongtai AIC's determination that the plaintiff's "Golden Arowana" brand Olive Fragrance Edible Blend Oil label specifically emphasized a valuable or characteristic ingredient was incorrect. 2. The defendant's enforcement procedure was erroneous. Whether a product complies with standards should be determined based on inspection data. The defendant imposed a penalty on the plaintiff without conducting an official inspection, which constituted a procedural violation. 3. The Penalty Decision applied the law incorrectly. This case should have applied the national food safety standards promulgated by the health administrative department of the State Council under the Food Safety Law. However, the standard applied by the defendant, GB7718-2004 General Standard for the Labeling of Prepackaged Foods, is not a national food safety standard. In summary, the plaintiff requested that the court revoke the Penalty Decision.

The plaintiff, Aokang Company, submitted the following evidence:
(1) The Penalty Decision, to prove the existence of the administrative act under review.
(2) The Administrative Reconsideration Decision No. [2012] 2 of Yancheng Administration for Industry and Commerce, to prove the situation regarding the administrative reconsideration filed against the penalty.
(3) The textbook "Implementation Guide for National Standards on Food Labeling" compiled by the Secretariat of the National Food Industry Standardization Technical Committee, to prove that only valuable or characteristic ingredients need to indicate the amount or content added.

The defendant, Dongtai AIC, argued: 1. The factual determination made by our Administration was correct. The plaintiff Aokang Company sold to Dongtai Guomao Qianjiahui Supermarket (hereinafter referred to as Qianjiahui Supermarket) the "Golden Arowana" brand Olive Fragrance Edible Blend Oil, on the front of whose label the word "Olive" prominently appeared, accompanied by an olive graphic, and a hang tag stated "Contains 100% extra virgin olive oil imported from Italy." However, the amount added was not indicated. This constituted a situation where a food label specifically emphasizes the addition of a valuable or characteristic ingredient without indicating the amount added. 2. Our Administration's penalty procedure was lawful. Issues of product quality need to be determined through technical inspection, but the content of food labels is clear at a glance and does not require inspection. 3. Our Administration's application of the law was accurate. GB7718-2004 General Standard for the Labeling of Prepackaged Foods, as a mandatory standard for food labeling, was deemed one of the food safety standards after the Food Safety Law came into effect, until it was replaced by GB7718-2011 General Standard for the Labeling of Prepackaged Foods. Therefore, the Penalty Decision issued by our Administration was proper, and we requested the court to uphold it.

The defendant, Dongtai AIC, submitted the following evidence:
(1) First set of evidence: Business licenses of the plaintiff Aokang Company and Qianjiahui Supermarket; on-site inspection records of Qianjiahui Supermarket; interrogation records of Xue Feng, an employee of Aokang Company, and Sheng Weihua, an employee of Qianjiahui Supermarket; letters of authorization from Aokang Company and Qianjiahui Supermarket; photographs taken by law enforcement officers of the defendant Dongtai AIC, etc., to prove that the label of the "Golden Arowana" brand Olive Fragrance Edible Blend Oil operated and sold by Aokang Company specifically emphasized the ingredient of olive oil but did not indicate the amount of olive oil added.
(2) Second set of evidence: A summary table of the operation of Olive Fragrance Edible Blend Oil from September 1, 2011, to February 29, 2012, prepared by Xue Feng and stamped with the seal of the plaintiff Aokang Company; a summary report of commodity sales and a summary report of inventory commodities, including Olive Fragrance Edible Blend Oil, from Qianjiahui Supermarket, to prove the purchase price, selling price, quantity, sales revenue, and net profit of the "Golden Arowana" brand Olive Fragrance Edible Blend Oil operated by Aokang Company.
(3) Third set of evidence: Case filing approval form, administrative penalty hearing notice, case investigation final report, case review form, record of discussion on major cases, administrative penalty decision approval form, administrative penalty decision and return receipt of service, Jiangsu Provincial receipt for confiscated fines, etc., to prove that the procedure for the penalty decision issued by the defendant Dongtai AIC was lawful.
(4) Fourth set of evidence: Other materials in this case, as well as the laws, regulations, and normative bases relied upon.

The Dongtai People's Court organized cross-examination of the evidence by both parties in accordance with the law.

The plaintiff, Aokang Company, raised no objection to the authenticity of the evidence provided by the defendant, Dongtai AIC, but did not accept the purpose of proof for the first and third sets of evidence. The defendant, Dongtai AIC, raised no objection to the authenticity of the evidence provided by the plaintiff, Aokang Company.

The Dongtai People's Court confirmed the evidence provided by the plaintiff, Aokang Company.

The Dongtai People's Court found in the first instance:

From September 1, 2011, to February 29, 2012, the plaintiff, Aokang Company, purchased 290 bottles of "Golden Arowana" brand Olive Fragrance Edible Blend Oil with a net content of 5 liters, and sold them to Qianjiahui Supermarket at a markup, generating sales revenue of RMB 34,800 and net profit of RMB 2,836.9.

On February 21, 2012, when law enforcement officers of the defendant, Dongtai AIC, conducted an inspection at Qianjiahui Supermarket, they discovered that the aforementioned "Golden Arowana" brand Olive Fragrance Edible Blend Oil did not indicate the amount of olive oil added.

It was further ascertained that the name of the aforementioned "Golden Arowana" brand Olive Fragrance Edible Blend Oil was "Olive Fragrance Edible Blend Oil." Its label featured the word "Olive," accompanied by an olive graphic, and the side of the label indicated "Ingredients: rapeseed oil, soybean oil, olive oil," and other contents. The hang tag contained the following description: "Golden Arowana Olive Fragrance Edible Blend Oil, contains 100% extra virgin olive oil imported from Italy, exuding a faint fragrance of olive fruit. In addition to being rich in multiple vitamins, monounsaturated fatty acids, and other healthful substances, its olive essence contains natural antioxidant components such as polyphenols, satisfying the pursuit of a natural and healthy high-quality life."

The defendant, Dongtai AIC, opened a case for investigation on February 27, 2012, and served the Administrative Penalty Hearing Notice No. [2012] 91503 on the plaintiff, Aokang Company, on May 9. The plaintiff did not make any statements or defenses within the statutory period, nor did it request a hearing. On May 15, the defendant served the Administrative Penalty Decision No. [2012] 298 on the plaintiff, determining that the plaintiff operated food whose labels did not comply with the provisions of the Food Safety Law, and imposed an administrative penalty of ordering corrections, confiscating illegal income of RMB 2,836.9, and imposing a fine of RMB 57,163.1, totaling a forfeiture and fine of RMB 60,000. The plaintiff, dissatisfied, applied for administrative reconsideration, and the Yancheng Administration for Industry and Commerce upheld the penalty decision upon reconsideration.

The issues in dispute in the first instance of this case were: (1) Whether the facts determined in the Penalty Decision were established, specifically whether the label of the "Golden Arowana" brand Olive Fragrance Edible Blend Oil operated by the plaintiff Aokang Company specifically emphasized a valuable or characteristic ingredient, and whether the label should have indicated the amount of olive oil added; (2) Whether the procedure of the penalty decision by the defendant Dongtai AIC was lawful, and whether technical inspection of the label in question was necessary; (3) Whether the application of law in the Penalty Decision was correct.

The Dongtai People's Court held in the first instance:

GB7718-2004 General Standard for the Labeling of Prepackaged Foods, which came into effect on October 1, 2005, stipulates that prepackaged foods are foods that are pre-packaged in predetermined quantities, or placed (filled) into containers, and directly provided to consumers; food labels are the text, graphics, symbols, and all descriptive matter on food packaging. Therefore, the "Golden Arowana" brand Olive Fragrance Edible Blend Oil operated by the plaintiff Aokang Company is a prepackaged food, and its label is a prepackaged food label.

GB7718-2004 General Standard for the Labeling of Prepackaged Foods stipulates: "All content on the label of prepackaged foods shall not introduce the food with false, misleading, or deceptive text, graphics, or other means; nor shall it use font size or color differences to mislead consumers." "If a food label or food instructions specifically emphasize the addition of one or more valuable or characteristic ingredients, the amount of the emphasized ingredient added shall be indicated." The term "emphasis" as used here means to give special prominence or stress. Generally, emphasis on something can be understood through names, color differences, different fonts, font sizes, graphics, arrangement order, textual descriptions, repeated appearance of the same content, or multiple contents pointing to the same subject. "Valuable or characteristic ingredients" refer to special ingredients that have a higher nutritional effect on the human body and are themselves different from ordinary ingredients. It is generally understood that the market price or nutritional content of such ingredients should be higher than that of other ingredients. In this case, the plaintiff Aokang Company argued that "Olive Fragrance" was an objective description of the product's physical attributes, not an emphasis on a particular ingredient. However, from the external packaging of the "Golden Arowana" brand Olive Fragrance Edible Blend Oil sold by the plaintiff, the label highlighted the word "Olive" through graphics, fonts, textual descriptions, and other means, emphasizing that the edible blend oil contained the ingredient of olive oil. Furthermore, the hang tag (a component of the food label) contained textual descriptions such as "Contains 100% extra virgin olive oil imported from Italy," which could easily mislead consumers when purchasing this edible blend oil. "Valuable or characteristic" is a common-sense judgment based on general understanding. Provided that "special emphasis" is satisfied, quantitative labeling should be carried out as long as either "valuable" or "characteristic" is present. Generally speaking, the market price or nutritional function of olive oil is higher than that of ordinary soybean oil, rapeseed oil, etc. Therefore, if olive oil is added to an edible blend oil, it can be determined that olive oil is a "valuable or characteristic ingredient." Consequently, the determination by the defendant Dongtai AIC that the "Golden Arowana" brand Olive Fragrance Edible Blend Oil sold by the plaintiff fell under the circumstance of specifically emphasizing the addition of a valuable or characteristic ingredient (olive oil) and should have indicated the amount of olive oil added could be established.

Article 60, paragraph 3 of the Food Safety Law stipulates that if industry and commerce authorities and other authorities at or above the county level need to inspect food during law enforcement, they shall entrust a food inspection institution to do so. Accordingly, industry and commerce authorities may, as needed, inspect food during specific law enforcement processes. In this case, the fact that the label of the "Golden Arowana" brand Olive Fragrance Edible Blend Oil sold by the plaintiff emphasized the addition of the olive oil ingredient without indicating the amount added could be determined through normal visual observation and cognition. Therefore, there was no need to entrust an inspection institution for testing. The defendant's failure to entrust testing was not illegal.

Article 20, item (4) of the Food Safety Law stipulates that food safety standards shall include requirements for labels, marks, and instructions related to food safety and nutrition. Article 22 stipulates that before the national food safety standards provided for in this Law are published, food producers and traders shall produce and trade food in accordance with the existing quality and safety standards for edible agricultural products, food hygiene standards, food quality standards, and relevant industry standards for food. In a response dated March 19, 2010, to the General Administration of Quality Supervision, Inspection and Quarantine's letter seeking clarification on legal application issues related to food safety standards, the Legislative Affairs Commission of the National People's Congress stated that before the national food safety standards are published, the relevant provisions of the Food Safety Law shall apply when investigating and punishing illegal acts of producing or trading food that does not comply with the existing quality and safety standards for edible agricultural products, food hygiene standards, food quality standards, and relevant industry standards for food. GB7718-2004 General Standard for the Labeling of Prepackaged Foods came into effect on October 1, 2005, the Food Safety Law came into effect on June 1, 2009, and the new version, GB7718-2011 General Standard for the Labeling of Prepackaged Foods, came into effect on April 20, 2012. The illegal acts of the plaintiff Aokang Company in this case occurred from September 2011 to February 2012. GB7718-2004 General Standard for the Labeling of Prepackaged Foods was one of the national food safety standards in effect at that time. Therefore, there was no impropriety in the defendant Dongtai AIC's application of GB7718-2004 General Standard for the Labeling of Prepackaged Foods to impose the administrative penalty on the plaintiff.

Accordingly, the Dongtai People's Court, pursuant to Article 42, paragraph 1, item (9) and Article 86, item (2) of the Food Safety Law, and Article 54, paragraph 1, item (1) of the Administrative Procedure Law, rendered a judgment on December 15, 2012:

Uphold the Administrative Penalty Decision No. [2012] 298 issued by the defendant Dongtai AIC.

Aokang Company, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Yancheng Intermediate People's Court.

The appellant, Aokang Company, appealed on the grounds that: (1) The application of law in the administrative penalty by the appellee Dongtai AIC was erroneous. GB7718-2004 General Standard for the Labeling of Prepackaged Foods was not formulated by the health administrative department of the State Council as required by the Food Safety Law and therefore should not be applied to this case. (2) Pursuant to Article 19 of the Standardization Law, disputes concerning whether a product complies with standards shall be resolved based on inspection data from inspection institutions. Dongtai AIC did not conduct any inspection during the penalty in this case, which violated legal provisions. (3) The first-instance court's determination of "valuable or characteristic ingredients" was erroneous. In summary, the first-instance judgment was erroneous, and the appellant requested the second-instance court to amend the judgment according to law.

The appellee, Dongtai AIC, argued: (1) The objective fact existed that the appellant Aokang Company sold food with labels that did not comply with the provisions of the Food Safety Law. (2) The appellee's application of the Food Safety Law and GB7718-2004 General Standard for the Labeling of Prepackaged Foods to impose the penalty on the appellant was correct in law, the penalty procedure was lawful, and the penalty amount was appropriate. Therefore, the appellee requested the second-instance court to dismiss the appeal and uphold the original judgment.

The Yancheng Intermediate People's Court, upon second-instance trial, confirmed the facts found in the first instance.

The issues in dispute in the second instance of this case were: (1) Whether the appellee Dongtai AIC, in imposing the penalty on the appellant, should have applied GB7718-2004 General Standard for the Labeling of Prepackaged Foods; (2) Whether the label of the "Golden Arowana" brand Olive Fragrance Edible Blend Oil sold by the appellant Aokang Company should have indicated the amount of olive oil added.

The Yancheng Intermediate People's Court held in the second instance:

Pursuant to Article 4, paragraph 3 of the Food Safety Law and Articles 15 and 20 of the Administrative Penalty Law, the appellee Dongtai AIC had the statutory authority to lawfully investigate and handle whether the act of the appellant Aokang Company in operating and selling the "Golden Arowana" brand Olive Fragrance Edible Blend Oil was illegal.

Article 20, item (4) of the Food Safety Law stipulates that food safety standards shall include requirements for labels, marks, and instructions related to food safety and nutrition. Therefore, the content and specific requirements of labels related to food safety and nutrition are part of the food safety standards. GB7718-2004 General Standard for the Labeling of Prepackaged Foods and GB7718-2011 General Standard for the Labeling of Prepackaged Foods are national food safety standards successively promulgated and implemented by relevant state authorities. They have a successive replacement relationship and are also part of the series of national standards for food labeling. GB7718-2011 General Standard for the Labeling of Prepackaged Foods was formulated by the health administrative department of the State Council and is clearly stated to be a national food safety standard. There is no doubt that for labels related to food safety and nutrition occurring after April 20, 2012, GB7718-2011 General Standard for the Labeling of Prepackaged Foods should apply. However, in this case, the illegal act of the appellant Aokang Company in operating and selling the Olive Fragrance Edible Blend Oil without indicating the amount of olive oil added occurred from September 2011 to February 2012. There was no impropriety in the appellee Dongtai AIC's application of GB7718-2004 General Standard for the Labeling of Prepackaged Foods, which was a valid legal norm (standard) at the time the illegal act occurred.

The appellant Aokang Company's argument that disputes concerning whether a product complies with standards should be resolved based on inspection data was contrary to the law. The penalty imposed by the appellee Dongtai AIC targeted the illegal act of food label marking, not whether the quality of the product itself complied with relevant standards. Therefore, there was no need for a specialized entrusted inspection in this case.

The appellant Aokang Company's argument that the "Olive" marking on the label did not constitute "valuable or characteristic" and that olive oil was not a valuable or characteristic ingredient was untenable. How to accurately determine "specifically emphasizing the addition of one or more valuable or characteristic ingredients" should be comprehensively analyzed and judged from the perspectives of the expression context, relative comparison, and public understanding. In this case, from the external packaging of the "Golden Arowana" brand Olive Fragrance Edible Blend Oil operated and sold by the appellant Aokang Company, the label highlighted the word "Olive" through graphics, fonts, textual descriptions, and other means, obviously emphasizing to consumers that the product contained the ingredient of olive oil. This practice itself, in fact, emphasized the value and characteristics of "Olive" in the product. GB7718-2004 General Standard for the Labeling of Prepackaged Foods stipulates: "If a food label or food instructions specifically emphasize the addition of one or more valuable or characteristic ingredients, the amount of the emphasized ingredient added shall be indicated." The appellant Aokang Company did not indicate the amount of olive oil added, which constituted a violation of food safety standards.

Accordingly, the Yancheng Intermediate People's Court, pursuant to Article 61, item (1) of the Administrative Procedure Law, rendered a judgment on May 9, 2013:

Dismiss the appeal and uphold the original judgment.

This judgment is final.
